definitions.definition: For each nonnegative integer k, Eucl(k)=R^k is the space of real k-tuples, with distance (sum_{j=1}^k |x_j-y_j|^2)^(1/2) and its Borel sigma algebra. The empty tuple is the sole point of Eucl(0). Eucl(k)×R is identified with Eucl(k+1) by adjoining the last coordinate; this identification uses the Euclidean distance sqrt(||x-y||_2^2+|t-u|^2).

definitions.type: diameter function on subsets of metric or extended metric spaces
definitions.definition: diam(A)=sup{dist(x,y): x,y in A}, as an extended nonnegative number, with supremum of the empty set zero. Thus diam(empty)=0. In ordinary Euclidean spaces a nonempty set of diameter zero is a singleton. Native ediam is this extended-valued diameter. Euclidean finite diameters are identified with their nonnegative real values.

binders.type: subset of a metric or extended metric space

definitions.type: positive exponent and scale Hausdorff contents and limiting Hausdorff measure on Euclidean sets
definitions.definition:
For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put

\[
H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
 A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
\qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
\]

Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero.

binders.type: countable family of subsets of the same Euclidean space

definitions.type: real exponent → Borel Hausdorff measure on any extended metric space
definitions.definition: muH(a) denotes the native unnormalized Borel Hausdorff measure MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure a. It is obtained by the metric outer-measure construction mkMetric with gauge r↦r^a on extended nonnegative diameters: at each positive scale take the maximal outer measure bounded by the gauge on all nonempty sets of at most that diameter, then take the supremum over scales and its Borel-measure realization. Values on arbitrary sets mean outer-measure values. Empty covering members cost zero and nonempty members cost diam^a with extended nonnegative-real powers; at a=0 a nonempty singleton has cost 1.

definitions.type: Hausdorff dimension of subsets of metric spaces, valued in [0,infinity]
definitions.definition: dimH(A), also written dim_H A, is the standard Hausdorff dimension: sup({a≥0 : muH(a)(A)=infinity}) in [0,infinity], where the supremum of an empty set is 0. This is the native dimH definition. The notation uses the empty-set dimension convention 0. Critical-exponent properties and agreement with the supplied positive-exponent diameter-cost measure are proof obligations, not extra assumptions.

binders.type: subset of an extended metric space

definitions.definition: F=E×I under the Euclidean identification in D001.
D=dimH(E), initially an extended nonnegative real. Real arithmetic involving D is used only after its finiteness is proved.

definitions.type: Lebesgue measure on R and associated integral notation
definitions.definition: lambda is the standard Lebesgue measure on R with its Borel measurable structure and the normalization by interval length. For a Borel set J, |J| denotes lambda(J). The symbol 1_J denotes its indicator, equal to 1 on J and 0 elsewhere. Integrals of nonnegative functions are extended Lebesgue integrals (native lintegral). Restriction to I is lambda restricted to [0,1]. The usual interval values are lambda(I)=1 and lambda((a,b))=b-a for a<b; only these interval values are used.

inputs.statement: 0≤D≤n, so D is finite. Also, for every s>0 and delta>0, H^s_delta(E)<infinity.

For any measurable space X, any measure nu on X, any countable type T, and any family f:T→X→[0,infinity], if every f(i) is nu-almost-everywhere measurable, then the nonnegative extended integral of sum_{i in T} f(i) equals sum_{i in T} of the nonnegative extended integrals of f(i). No finiteness or sigma-finiteness assumption is required.

hypotheses: X is a measurable space and nu a measure on it.
For every i in T, f(i) is nu-almost-everywhere measurable.

output.statement: For every real s>0 and delta>0, H^s_delta(E)≤H^{s+1}_delta(F).

locals.declaration: Consider an arbitrary countable family V, temporarily assumed in L1 to be a delta-cover of F.
Enumerate the original family by N, allowing empty padding; let T be the indices of its nonempty members. All i-series below range over T.
For i in T set rho_i=diam(V_i).

locals.type: T-indexed family of subsets of Eucl(n)
locals.declaration: For i in T let A_i be the first-coordinate projection of V_i.

locals.type: T-indexed family of subsets of R
locals.declaration: For i in T let B_i be the last-coordinate projection of V_i.
Set c=H^s_delta(E), initially as an extended nonnegative real.

locals.type: T-indexed family of open bounded intervals in R
locals.declaration: Set J_i=(inf B_i-eta_i/2,sup B_i+eta_i/2). F001 supplies bounded nonempty B_i.
Define f_i(t)=rho_i^s 1_{J_i}(t), with its finite nonnegative coefficient included in the extended nonnegative reals.
Fix t in I to check the slice cover.

argument.text: Fix s>0 and delta>0. Take any countable family V and introduce L1: V is a delta-cover of F. Enumerate it with possible empty padding, discard empties, and write T⊆N for the remaining indices; all i-series in this inference are over T. Define rho_i=diam(V_i), and A_i and B_i as its first and last coordinate projections. By the Euclidean distance formula, each coordinate projection is 1-Lipschitz. Thus A_i and B_i are nonempty and have diameter ≤rho_i≤delta. In particular B_i is bounded, with finite infimum and supremum and sup B_i-inf B_i≤rho_i. Put c=H^s_delta(E). By N002, c is finite.

produces.statement: c<infinity; for every i in T, 0≤rho_i≤delta, diam(A_i)≤rho_i, and B_i is nonempty and bounded with sup B_i-inf B_i≤rho_i.

argument.text: For arbitrary epsilon>0 set eta_i=epsilon 2^(-i-1)/(1+rho_i^s)>0. By F001 define the bounded open interval J_i=(inf B_i-eta_i/2,sup B_i+eta_i/2). It contains B_i and its length is sup B_i-inf B_i+eta_i≤rho_i+eta_i. This construction also works when rho_i=0. No measurability of V_i, A_i or B_i is asserted or required. Furthermore sum_i eta_i rho_i^s≤epsilon sum_{i in T}2^(-i-1)≤epsilon, since 0≤rho_i^s/(1+rho_i^s)≤1.

produces.statement: For every i in T, B_i⊆J_i, J_i is a bounded open interval and |J_i∩I|≤rho_i+eta_i; also sum_{i in T} eta_i rho_i^s≤epsilon.

argument.text: For each t∈I, the A_i with t∈J_i cover E. Indeed, for each x∈E, the point (x,t)∈F lies in some V_i, so x∈A_i and t∈B_i⊆J_i. Their diameters are ≤rho_i≤delta by F001. The definition of the infimum H^s_delta(E) therefore gives c≤sum_i rho_i^s 1_{J_i}(t). Define f_i(t)=rho_i^s 1_{J_i}(t). Each f_i is a nonnegative Borel measurable function: J_i is open and the coefficient rho_i^s is finite. Thus it is almost-everywhere measurable for lambda restricted to I.

produces.statement: For every t0∈I, c≤sum_{i in T} f_i(t0). Every f_i is Borel measurable, hence almost-everywhere measurable for lambda restricted to I.

argument.text: Integrate F003 over I, whose Lebesgue measure is one. Monotonicity of the nonnegative integral gives c≤integral_I sum_i f_i. Apply M001 on R with measure lambda restricted to I, index type T, and this f: T is countable as a subset of N, and F003 gives the required almost-everywhere measurability. We obtain c≤sum_i integral_I f_i=sum_i rho_i^s |J_i∩I|. The last equality is the integral formula for a nonnegative constant times a measurable indicator, which follows directly from the simple-function definition of the integral. By F002, c≤sum_i rho_i^s |J_i∩I|≤sum_i rho_i^(s+1)+sum_i eta_i rho_i^s≤sum_i rho_i^(s+1)+epsilon. Here rho_i^s rho_i=rho_i^(s+1) also at rho_i=0 since s>0; nonnegative series permit termwise comparison and splitting.

produces.statement: For every e0>0, c≤sum_{i in T} rho_i^(s+1)+e0.

argument.text: The construction works for every epsilon>0, and F004 has eliminated the private intervals and their dependence on epsilon. If sum_i rho_i^(s+1)=infinity, c≤that series is immediate. If it is finite, the inequalities in F004 for all e0>0 and the finite c from F001 allow e0 to decrease to zero, giving c≤sum_i rho_i^(s+1). Thus in both cases c≤the (s+1)-cost of the original cover, since deleted empties have zero cost.

Discharge L1: every countable delta-cover V of F has (s+1)-cost at least c=H^s_delta(E). Taking its infimum proves H^s_delta(E)≤H^{s+1}_delta(F). This is valid even if no admissible cover existed, when the right infimum would be infinity. Quantify s>0 and delta>0 to obtain the exported claim. No object depending on a particular V or epsilon occurs in this output.
